Hadrian. A Roman emperor who ruled from AD 117 to 138, known as the third of the Five Good Emperors. Unlike his expansionist predecessor Trajan, Hadrian focused on consolidating the empire and securing its borders. He was a passionate admirer of Greek culture and spent more than half of his reign travelling extensively throughout the empire's provinces.

He ordered the construction of Hadrian's Wall in northern Britain to mark the empire's frontier and defend against the Picts. He rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome, constructing the famous domed structure with a central oculus that stands to this day. He crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt in Judaea, devastating the Jewish population and renaming the province Syria Palaestina. He deeply grieved the death of his Greek lover Antinous, who drowned in the Nile, and subsequently deified him and founded the city of Antinoöpolis in his honour. He abandoned Trajan's recent conquests in Mesopotamia and Armenia, judging them too difficult to defend.

His predecessor and fellow Spaniard was Trajan, his adoptive father, though Hadrian largely abandoned Trajan's aggressive expansionist policies. His adopted heir and successor was Antoninus Pius, whom he required to adopt Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus in turn.
